3. The Society stated that the acquisition was however challenged by a few persons before this Court and the acquisition was set aside and was also confirmed by the Hon'ble Supreme Court.

The Society stated that the Apex Court had directed that the State Government had to redeliver the property to the land owners and the monies paid by the Society was to be returned to it and a further direction was also issued that the land-owners should pay the money to the Society.

4. It was stated that as a matter of fact, an agreement had been entered into between the Society and the land owners, with the assistance of S.Ramachandran-- Engineering Contractor, whereby, the Society had agreed to pay certain sums to the land-owners apart from what had been paid by the Society through the Government.

It was stated that since there was a direction by the Apex Court to the Government to hand-over the possession of the acquired lands to its land-owners, who were in turn required to return the money they had received from the Government and the Government had failed to abide by the said order, they were constrained to file Writ Petition No.26197 of 1996 before The Bangalore City Chikpet House ... vs Nanjappa Dead By Lrs on 15 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/132413711/

5. It was contended that the land-owners did not return the amount paid under the agreement and hence, the Society was constrained to issue legal notice to them calling upon them to pay the monies paid under the agreement.
6.
It is also not in dispute that the money which the Society had deposited before the Land Acquisition Officer was in fact returned to them pursuant to filing of the Writ Petition.
The possession was also redelivered to the land- owners.
7. The land-owners and the legal heirs of S.Ramachandran contested the suit by filing their written statement.

8. The land-owners contended that the Society had paid them certain compensation and pursuant to the order of the Hon'ble Supreme Court, the compensation that had been paid was returned by the land-owners to the Land Acquisition Officer and the Land Acquisition Officer accepted the amount and had also issued an Official Memorandum to that effect.
It was also contended that since the money that the land-owners had received as compensation was returned by them, possession was also restored to them.
9. The legal heirs of Ramachandran contended that the suit was not maintainable as it was hopelessly barred by time.

It was stated that Ramachandran was not a party to the agreement between the Society and the land-owners and the agreement between Ramachandran and the Society was held to be void and opposed to the public policy by the Hon'ble Supreme Court and therefore, the Society could not seek to enforce the said agreement and seek for refund of the money paid under the void contract.
10. The Trial Court on consideration of the pleadings framed necessary issues.
11. On behalf of the Society, its Secretary was examined in all the suits and fourteen documents were admitted in evidence and marked them as exhibits (in O.S. Nos.1592 of 2001).

12. On behalf of the land-owners, either the land-owner or their General Power of Attorney holder was examined and on behalf of the legal representatives of Ramachandran, his son--R.Shridhar (defendant No.4 in O.S. No.4210 of 2001 and defendant No.3 in O.S. Nos.1592 and 1581 of 2001)
was examined and four documents were admitted in evidence and marked them as exhibits (in O.S.
Nos.1592 of 2001).

13. The Trial Court on consideration of the evidence adduced, came to the conclusion that the land-owners had received the sum as contended by the Society and the monies paid by the land-owners to the Land Acquisition Officer did not tantamount to the refund of the amount which had been received by the land-owners.

However, the Trial Court came to the conclusion that the Society had challenged the quashing of the acquisition before the Hon'ble Supreme court in S.L.P.

sentences.text: However, since the suits had been instituted in 2001, they were clearly barred by time and accordingly, the Trial Court proceeded to dismiss the suits.

14. Sri.S.Krishnaswamy, learned counsel appearing for the Society contended that when the Trial Court had recorded a finding that monies had been paid by the Society and it was also not in dispute that the acquisition - 10 - did not materialize and was in fact quashed, it was incumbent upon the Trial Court to decree the suit and prevent an unjust enrichment to the land-owners.

He also contended that the Society could file the suit only after possession was delivered and not before and therefore, the date of disposal of the Special Leave Petition would be of no consequence and the observation that the suit was barred by limitation could not be accepted.
15. Learned counsel appearing for the land-owners, on the other hand, contended that the judgment and decree of the Trial court cannot be found fault with.

Learned counsel submitted that the land-owners deposited the money that they had received in the year 1997 and the payment of this sum was also acknowledged by the Land Acquisition Officer and it was only thereafter that possession was restored to them.

He submitted that since the money was returned in the year 1997 and possession was also restored in 1997, even if the argument of the Society were to be accepted,
the suits would nevertheless - 11 - be barred by time, since it had been filed only in the year 2001.
16.

Having regard to the arguments advanced by the learned counsel for both the parties, the only point that arises for consideration in these appeals is as to whether the Society was entitled to claim for refund of the monies that it had paid to the land-owners under the agreements apart from the sums that it had deposited before the Special Land Acquisition Officer.

17. It cannot be in dispute that when the lands are acquired on behalf of a Company under the Land Acquisition Act, the Company is required to deposit the estimated cost of acquisition for the lands with the State and enter into a contract which was prescribed under the statute.

18. In law, the liability of the Company for acqusition of lands would be the sum determined by the Land - 12 - The Bangalore City Chikpet House ... vs Nanjappa Dead By Lrs on 15 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/132413711/

sentences.text: 6 Acquisition Officer.
It is also not in dispute that a Society on whose behalf lands are proposed to be acquired is also a Company within the meaning of the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act.

If a Company goes beyond the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act and pays extra amounts to the land-owners to facilitate the acquisition, the question as to whether the Company can seek for refund of the said amount, would also have to be considered.
19. In this case, the Society admits that at the instance of a middle-man, i.e., S.Ramachandran, the monies were paid to the land-owners.
In fact, the receipts that were relied upon were receipts which were executed by the land-owners in favour of S.Ramachandran.
It was therefore clear that the monies that were received by the land-owners were essentially monies that were paid to them by S.Ramachandran.

20. The Society, which claims to have had an understanding or a liaison with Ramachandran, for the - 13 - purpose of paying money to the land-owners to facilitate acquisition, was basically trying to by-pass the entire procedure prescribed under the Land Acquisition Act and was trying to buy the silence of the land-owners.
In my view, the monies paid for this purpose cannot be said to be a contract entered into for a lawful consideration and object.

21. The entire agreement was basically entered into to ensure that the acquisition was not challenged and this was not permissible under the agreement which the Society had entered into with the State.

The Society was essentially required to deposit the cost of acquisition as determined by the State and if it had decided to forego that contract and approach the land-owners directly through a middleman, it would have to face consequence for attempting to achieve an objective,
which was not permissible in law.
Viewed in this light of the matter, the entering of agreement by the Society would itself be - 14 - opposed to the public policy and therefore, would be unenforceable.
22. Apart from the above legal consideration, it has to be noticed here that the land-owners repaid the monies to the Special Land Acquisition Officer in the year 1997.
This contention of the land-owners that they repaid the monies in the year 1997 is not seriously in dispute.
It is also not seriously disputed that the possession was redelivered to the land-owners in the year 1997 after they deposited the monies with the Land Acquisition Officer.
However, the suits have been filed only in the year 2001 i.e., clearly after a period of three years.

23. Even if the argument of the learned counsel for the Society is to be accepted that the Society became entitled for the suit for recovery at the time of delivery of possession, since the possession was delivered after the amounts were repaid in the year 1997, it is clear that the suits filed in the year 2001 were barred by limitation.
